title: Properties of the Transform
intro: Each operation on a signal in time does something simple to X(s): a delay multiplies by an exponential, a damping factor slides the plane, a derivative multiplies by s, a convolution multiplies two surfaces. The two value theorems read the start and the end of a signal off the transform.

blocks.text: This page goes through the rules one at a time: the move in time, what it does to $X(s)$, and what it does to the picture. $\mathcal{R}$ stands for the region of convergence of $X(s)$. Throughout, $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(s)$ means the two are a transform pair.
Linearity

The integral is linear, so the transform of a sum is the sum of the transforms. The poles of the sum are the poles of the parts, and the region is at least where both converge; it can be larger if a pole cancels. Every other rule below is built on this one, and it is what makes partial fractions work on the page Inverting the Transform (#/math/laplace-transform/inverse).
Delay: multiplying by an exponential

Delaying a signal by $T$ seconds multiplies its transform by $e^{-sT}$. Check it with the impulse: $\delta(t)$ has $X(s) = 1$, so $\delta(t-1)$ has $e^{-s}$, as the page Points of the s-Plane (#/math/laplace-transform/s-plane) found directly. The pulse $u(t) - u(t-3)$ is a step minus a step delayed by three seconds, so its transform is $1/s - e^{-3s}/s = (1 - e^{-3s})/s$.

On the imaginary axis $|e^{-j\omega T}| = 1$, so the magnitude response does not change; only the phase picks up $-\omega T$. Off the axis it does: $|e^{-sT}| = e^{-\sigma T}$, a tilt of the whole surface, $8.69\,T$ dB per unit of $\sigma$. The ROC is unchanged.

widget.title: A step and its delayed copy

blocks.text: The pulse is a step $1/s$ plus a delayed, negated step $-e^{-3s}/s$. Look at the s-plane panel: the step alone would have a pole at 0 and the region $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. Here the pole is gone: at $s = 0$ the two terms cancel and $X(0) = 3$, the area of the pulse. Instead there are zeros on the imaginary axis at $\omega = 2\pi k/3$. Sweep ω: the response panel hits the floor at $\omega = 2.09$ rad/s. Then compare the right and left sides of the surface: the delay $e^{-3s}$ is what makes the left side climb, since $|e^{-3s}| = e^{-3\sigma}$ is $20$ at $\sigma = -1$ and $0.05$ at $\sigma = 1$.
Multiplying by an exponential: sliding the plane

Replacing $s$ by $s + a$ moves every pole and zero by $-a$, to the left by $a$. Take the cosine $\cos(\omega_0 t)u(t)$, which has $X(s) = s/(s^2 + \omega_0^2)$: poles at $\pm j\omega_0$ on the axis, a zero at 0, region $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. Multiplying by $e^{-at}$ gives the damped cosine with $(s + a)/((s + a)^2 + \omega_0^2)$: poles at $-a \pm j\omega_0$, a zero at $-a$, region $\operatorname{Re} s > -a$. The whole picture has slid left by $a$. This is the same trick that gave a decaying exponential from the step: $u(t) \leftrightarrow 1/s$ and $e^{-at}u(t) \leftrightarrow 1/(s+a)$.
The slide is horizontal only, because $e^{-at}$ is real. A complex factor $e^{j\omega_1 t}$ would slide the plane up by $\omega_1$ as well, which is the modulation rule of Fourier analysis.

With Decay rate a at 0 this is the plain cosine: poles at $\pm j1.5$ on the imaginary axis, a zero at the origin, and the region just touching the axis. Drag a to 0.5: the poles, the zero and the shaded region all move left by $0.5$ together, to $-0.5 \pm j1.5$, $-0.5$ and $\operatorname{Re} s > -0.5$. Drag it to 1 and the poles are at $-1 \pm j1.5$. The surface keeps its shape and slides; the axis, which stayed put, now cuts through a different part of it.
Scaling

Playing the signal twice as fast ($c = 2$) pulls every pole twice as far from the origin. For $e^{-t}u(t)$, with a pole at $-1$, the signal $e^{-2t}u(t)$ is the sped-up copy: $\tfrac12 \cdot 1/(s/2 + 1) = 1/(s + 2)$. A faster signal has a broader spread of frequencies; a slower one packs into a narrower band. This is the first hint of the uncertainty principle on the page Properties of the Transform (#/math/fourier-transform/properties).
Differentiation and integration

These rules use the one-sided transform, where the integral starts at $0^-$, just before the switch-on, so that initial conditions can be carried. Differentiating multiplies by $s$ and subtracts the starting value. Check it on $e^{-at}u(t)$: $x(0^-) = 0$, so the derivative has transform $s/(s+a) = 1 - a/(s+a)$. In time that is $\delta(t) - a e^{-at}u(t)$, which is right: the jump at $t = 0$ is an impulse, and after it the signal decays with slope $-a$. Integrating divides by $s$: $\int_0^t e^{-\tau}d\tau = 1 - e^{-t}$ has $\frac{1}{s(s+1)} = \frac1s - \frac1{s+1}$.

This is why the Laplace transform turns calculus into algebra, and the page Solving Differential Equations (#/math/laplace-transform/differential-equations) uses it for exactly that. For a second derivative, apply the rule twice: $s^2 X(s) - s\,x(0^-) - x'(0^-)$.
Convolution: stacking surfaces

Convolving in time multiplies the transforms. The poles and zeros of the two simply pile together in one plot. In decibels the surfaces add: two systems in a row have a response, in dB, equal to the sum of their responses. Take $e^{-t}u(t) \leftrightarrow 1/(s+1)$ and $e^{-2t}u(t) \leftrightarrow 1/(s+2)$. The product is $1/((s+1)(s+2)) = 1/(s+1) - 1/(s+2)$, so the convolution is $e^{-t} - e^{-2t}$ for $t \ge 0$. Evaluating directly, $\int_0^t e^{-\tau}e^{-2(t-\tau)}d\tau = e^{-2t}(e^{t} - 1) = e^{-t} - e^{-2t}$, which agrees. At $t = 1$ it is $0.368 - 0.135 = 0.2325$; it peaks at $t = \ln 2 = 0.693$ with value $0.25$. A pole of one factor can cancel a zero of the other, and then the region can grow.
The value theorems

The first reads the signal's value just after the start from the far-away height of the surface; it needs $X(s)$ to go to zero at infinity, because otherwise there is an impulse at $t = 0$. The second reads the value it settles to from the behaviour near the origin; it needs every pole of $sX(s)$ to be strictly in the left half-plane, since otherwise the signal does not settle at all. As an example, $X(s) = 5/(s(s+2))$: $sX = 5/(s+2)$, which is $0$ as $s \to \infty$, so $x(0^+) = 0$, and $5/2 = 2.5$ as $s \to 0$, so $x(\infty) = 2.5$. The actual signal is $2.5(1 - e^{-2t})$, which is $0$ at the start, $2.16$ at $t = 1$, and tends to $2.5$.

The conditions matter. For $X(s) = 1/(s^2 + 1)$, $sX \to 0$ as $s \to 0$, but the signal is $\sin t$, which does not settle. For $1/(s-1)$, $sX \to 0$ too, and the signal is $e^{t}$, which diverges. Each fails the condition: the poles are on the axis, and to the right of it.
Problems

blocks.title: Shift and slide
blocks.text: Given $e^{-2t}u(t) \leftrightarrow 1/(s+2)$, find the transform of $e^{-2t}u(t-1)$ and of $e^{-t}\,e^{-2t}u(t)$.
solution: The first: $e^{-2t}u(t-1) = e^{-2}\,e^{-2(t-1)}u(t-1)$, which is the signal delayed by 1 and scaled by $e^{-2} = 0.135$: $X(s) = e^{-2}\,e^{-s}/(s+2) = 0.135\,e^{-s}/(s+2)$.
The second: $e^{-t}e^{-2t}u(t) = e^{-3t}u(t)$, so $1/(s+3)$ with region $\operatorname{Re} s > -3$. The pole slid left by 1, from $-2$ to $-3$.

blocks.title: Use the theorems
blocks.text: $X(s) = \dfrac{6}{s(s+1)(s+2)}$. Find $x(0^+)$ and $x(\infty)$, and check them against the signal.
solution: $sX(s) = 6/((s+1)(s+2))$ tends to $0$ at infinity and to $6/2 = 3$ at 0. Its poles, $-1$ and $-2$, are in the left half-plane, so both theorems apply: $x(0^+) = 0$, $x(\infty) = 3$.
Partial fractions give $3/s - 6/(s+1) + 3/(s+2)$, so $x(t) = 3 - 6e^{-t} + 3e^{-2t}$. At $t = 0$ that is $3 - 6 + 3 = 0$ and at $t = 1$ it is $1.199$; as $t \to \infty$ it is $3$.

blocks.title: A step through a filter
blocks.text: A unit step enters a system with impulse response $e^{-t}u(t)$. What is the output?
solution: The output is the convolution, whose transform is $\dfrac{1}{s}\cdot\dfrac{1}{s+1} = \dfrac1s - \dfrac1{s+1}$. So $y(t) = 1 - e^{-t}$ for $t \ge 0$: it starts at $0$ and settles at $1$. The final value theorem agrees: $sY = 1/(s+1) \to 1$.
